items.title: Generative Forecasting from Coarse Observations: Does Cascading Help?
items.summary: We study probabilistic forecasting of dynamical systems such as fluids and waves from coarse observations. Since the unseen fine scales influence the dynamics, the same coarse initial state can evolve into a whole distribution of futures. Generative forecasters may produce visually plausible samples, but it is hard to tell whether they sample the right conditional distribution, since trajectory data contain a single future for each initial state. We address this problem by generating reference data in a hierarchical way: for each coarse initial state, we generate many different fine-scale components and numerically evolve the full states. Using these conditional ensembles, we show that standard diffusion models and stochastic interpolants can make substantial distributional errors when trained over the full forecast horizon with finite data and model capacity, despite being exact in principle. We then show that cascading shorter forecasts greatly reduces these errors for the turbulent flows and waves we study, but we also find and characterize cases in which it hurts. Since the coarse process is not Markov, cascading discards information about the unresolved fine scales even with exact transitions. To understand this, we propose a solvable analytic model which shows that the optimal cascade depth decreases as the coupling between the unresolved and observed scales gets...

items.title: When Does Causality Help in Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection?
items.summary: Causality-aware scoring is common in multivariate time-series anomaly detection, yet the literature rarely states when it helps. Holding one causality-guided autoencoder (DeCauAE) fixed, we vary graph quality, anomaly type and protocol against ground truth. Graph quality fixes the payoff: on a twenty-variable DAG the gain over a graph-free autoencoder decays as the graph is corrupted. Anomaly type fixes the target: the structural factor lifts window F1 from 0.800 to 0.976 where anomalies break conditional structure, and its advantage vanishes below a break severity s 0.3. Protocol fixes the ranking: point-adjusted F1 lets a random score match the full model, while range-aware VUS separates the autoencoder family from the classical baselines. On real benchmarks the causal module pays only where density makes a system eligible and cross-subsample reproducibility selects entities inside it; enabling it everywhere costs 0.012 VUS-ROC. The structural factor also transfers to classical detectors .

items.title: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
items.summary: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. We ask whether this omission comes from the network or from the training objective. In multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, nnU-Net trained with its default Dice and cross-entropy loss produces almost no response to most of the small lesions it misses, so no decision threshold recovers them, and four other architectures trained with the same loss detect no more of them. We therefore change only the objective. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. items.title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
items.summary: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders...

items.title: TwoPass: Draft-Guided Few-Step Video Prediction for Robotic Manipulation
items.summary: Action-conditioned video prediction lets robots anticipate the visual consequences of their actions for planning and policy evaluation. Existing predictors denoise each future from noise without using their own estimate of it, which limits the quality of the predicted future, in particular of the manipulated objects, and requires many network calls. We present TwoPass, a self-conditioned training-and-inference framework that keeps the standard flow-matching objective. Self-Generated Draft Training supplies a detached clean-video estimate from the shared network as conditioning at the same noisy state. A Refinement-Only Late Adapter applies a dedicated residual transformation when a draft is present. At inference, Draft-Reuse Iterative Refinement obtains both a solver update and the next draft from each velocity prediction, requiring as few as 4 function evaluations (NFE) per video chunk. Training samples discrete solver-query noise levels and updates the pretrained backbone. Extensive experiments on Bridge and Language Table show that TwoPass achieves state-of-the-art results with 4 NFE, far fewer than the 50-59 calls of existing predictors.
